opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The honest answer is that the models themselves have gotten remarkably capable. If you look at any single step an agent takes, whether that's writing a bit of code, searching for something, or summarizing a document, the model is usually pretty good at it. The problem is compounding. If each step is 95% reliable and you chain twenty of them together, you're suddenly in a world where the whole task fails more often than it succeeds. So reliability for multistep work is really a different problem from reliability for single-turn chat.

I'd break what's needed into a few buckets.

The first is training models specifically for long-horizon work. A lot of the progress we've seen comes from reinforcement learning on real tasks in real environments, where the model learns to recover from mistakes. That's underrated. Good agents aren't the ones that never make errors. They're the ones that notice when something went wrong, back up, and try a different approach, the way a good engineer does when a test fails. You only get that behavior if you train on trajectories where things actually go wrong.

The second is the environment and tooling around the model. People sometimes treat the agent as just the model, but in practice a huge amount of reliability comes from the harness: what tools it has access to, how well those tools are designed, how context is managed over a long task, and whether the agent can check its own work. If an agent can run tests, look at the output, and verify things, it gets dramatically more reliable than one that's working blind.

The third, and maybe the most important for actual delegation, is the human interface. Delegation is fundamentally about trust, and trust gets built incrementally. You don't hand a new hire your most critical project on day one. You give them something scoped, you see how they do, and you expand from there. Agents need the same thing. They need to be transparent about what they did and why, ask for clarification when a request is genuinely ambiguous instead of guessing, and be honest about uncertainty, so they say "I couldn't get this part working" rather than papering over it. An agent that's 90% reliable but tells you exactly where the 10% is can be more useful than one that's 95% reliable and silently wrong the rest of the time.

And then there's evaluation, which is where I've spent a lot of my career. You can't improve what you can't measure, and measuring agent performance on open-ended, multistep tasks is really hard. Static benchmarks saturate quickly and don't reflect what people actually do. The teams making the most progress are building evals that look like real work, and they're really disciplined about looking at failure cases, not just aggregate scores.

So I don't think there's one silver bullet. It's better training for recovery and long horizons, better harnesses, interfaces designed around building trust, and much better evaluation, all moving together. But I'm optimistic. The trajectory over the last couple of years has been pretty steep, and people are already delegating real work to agents that they wouldn't have dreamed of handing off not long ago.

r002.rationale: It explains that chaining individually 95%-reliable steps makes the overall task fail more often than it succeeds.

r003.rationale: It calls for training models specifically for long-horizon work and describes reinforcement learning on real tasks and trajectories, including failures.

r004.rationale: It says training on trajectories where things go wrong teaches agents to notice errors, back up, and try a different approach during execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because it's basically the core problem we're working on at OpenPipe. The way I'd frame it is: the models are already smart enough to do most of the individual steps in these workflows. If you ask a frontier model to write a SQL query, or summarize a document, or decide which tool to call next, it'll get it right most of the time. The problem is "most of the time" doesn't compound well. If you've got a twenty-step task and each step is 95% reliable, you're at something like a one-in-three chance of making it to the end without a mistake. And nobody's going to delegate real work to something that fails two-thirds of the time.

So I think there are a few pieces that need to come together. The first one, which I think is underrated, is just having a really good definition of what success looks like. A lot of teams building agents don't actually have evals that reflect the task they care about. They have vibes. And you can't make something reliable if you can't measure whether it's reliable. So step one is almost boring: build the dataset, build the grader, figure out what "done correctly" means for your specific use case.

The second piece is that I don't think prompting alone gets you there. You can get pretty far with prompt engineering and better scaffolding, but at some point you hit a ceiling where the model just doesn't have the context or the judgment for your particular domain. And that's where I think training comes back in, specifically reinforcement learning on the agent's actual task. You let the model attempt the task many times, you reward the trajectories that succeed, and you end up with a model that's tuned to your environment, your tools, your failure modes. We've seen that take agents from "works in a demo" to something you can actually put in production, and the gap between those two is enormous.

And then the third thing, which is more of a product observation, is that reliability isn't just a model property, it's a system property. The best agents I've seen have really good mechanisms for recognizing when they're uncertain and either checking their work or pulling a human in. It's not that the human is doing the task, it's that the agent knows the boundaries of what it can handle. That's actually something you can train for too, but it's also a design choice about where you put the checkpoints.

So if I had to summarize it: measure the thing, train on the thing, and build the system so that the inevitable mistakes get caught before they cost anybody anything. The models are going to keep getting better, but I don't think any of those three pieces go away.

r001.rationale: It contrasts agents that “work in a demo” with agents reliable enough to put in production and delegate real work to.

r002.rationale: It explains that errors compound across steps and illustrates this with a 20-step task whose 95%-reliable steps yield about a one-in-three chance of finishing without a mistake.

r003.rationale: It identifies reinforcement learning on the agent’s actual task, with repeated task attempts and rewarded successful trajectories, as a way to improve reliability.

r004.rationale: It mentions tuning to failure modes and catching mistakes, but does not explain that encountering failures during training teaches agents to recover from failures during execution.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that reliability has to be measured at the level of the whole task. An agent can look impressive on individual steps, but if it makes a small mistake early and then builds on that mistake, the final result can be completely wrong. And as you ask it to do more steps, there are more opportunities for that to happen.

So you need a way to evaluate whether it actually accomplished what the user wanted, using tasks that are representative of the work people will delegate. Then you need to look at the failures: Was it missing information? Did it use the wrong tool? Did it fail to check its work? Those are different problems, and they call for different fixes.

I also think a reliable agent needs to know when to stop and ask for help. Delegation doesn’t necessarily mean zero human involvement. It means I don’t have to supervise every action, and I can trust the system to bring me back in when there’s a decision it can’t safely make on its own.

r001.rationale: It contrasts agents that look impressive on individual steps with whether they accomplish the whole task users delegate.

r002.rationale: It says an early small mistake can be built upon and that more steps create more opportunities for errors.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluating delegated tasks and diagnosing failures, but does not identify direct end-to-end training on agentic workflows as a missing ingredient.

r004.rationale: It does not say that encountering failures during training teaches agents to recover during execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is closing the loop between what the agent does and whether it actually accomplished the task. A model can produce a very plausible sequence of actions, but that’s different from reliably getting the outcome you wanted.

With multistep work, small errors compound. So you need ways for the agent to check its progress, recognize when something went wrong, and recover. And you need to evaluate the whole workflow on realistic tasks, including the messy cases where a tool fails or the instructions are ambiguous.

There’s also a question of knowing when to ask for help. I don’t think reliable delegation means the agent never comes back to you. It means it handles what it can, asks a useful question when it’s stuck, and gives you enough visibility to trust the result. Better models help, but that feedback and evaluation infrastructure is a big part of making the system dependable.

r001.rationale: It contrasts producing a plausible sequence of actions with reliably achieving the desired outcome, in the context of multistep delegation.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says small errors compound in multistep work.

r003.rationale: It discusses evaluation and feedback infrastructure, but does not identify direct end-to-end training on agent workflows as a missing ingredient.

r004.rationale: It mentions recovering when execution goes wrong, but does not say that failures encountered during training teach execution-time recovery.
